samf-junior-2012-r2-01.title: Compare with all 6s
samf-junior-2012-r2-01.body:
If no code were $7$ the maximum total would be $8\cdot6=48<50$. Each $7$ instead of a $6$ adds $1$, so we need at least $2$ sevens. Two sevens and six $6$s give $14+36=50$. 

**Answer: (E) 2**

samf-junior-2012-r2-02.title: Percentages
samf-junior-2012-r2-02.body:
After the friend he has $50\%$. Charity gets $10\%$ of that, i.e. $5\%$ of the original. He keeps $50-5=45\%$.

**Answer: (E) 45**

samf-junior-2012-r2-03.title: Use the divisibility rules
samf-junior-2012-r2-03.body:
Divisible by $5$: $Y\in\{0,5\}$. Divisible by $4$: the last two digits $8Y$ must be a multiple of $4$; $80$ works but $85$ does not, so $Y=0$. Divisible by $9$: the digit sum $2+4+X+8+0=14+X$ must be a multiple of $9$, so $X=4$. Then $X+Y=4$ (the number is $24480=9\cdot2720$).

**Answer: (E) 4**

samf-junior-2012-r2-04.title: Inscribed angle
samf-junior-2012-r2-04.body:
The vertices lie on a circle and the sides of the regular hexagon subtend arcs of $60^\circ$. The angle $RPS$ is an inscribed angle subtending the side $RS$, so $x=\frac12\cdot60^\circ=30^\circ$.

**Answer: (B) 30°**

samf-junior-2012-r2-04.title: Parallel lines
samf-junior-2012-r2-04.body:
Each interior angle is $120^\circ$, so in isosceles triangle $QPR$ we have $\angle QRP=30^\circ$. Since $PS\parallel QR$, $x=\angle QRP=30^\circ$.

**Answer: (B) 30°**

samf-junior-2012-r2-05.title: Remove the brackets
samf-junior-2012-r2-05.body:
Removing the brackets reverses the signs inside each bracket alternately, giving $1-2+3-4+\dots+99-100=(1-2)+(3-4)+\dots+(99-100)=50\cdot(-1)=-50$.

**Answer: (A) $-50$**

samf-junior-2012-r2-06.title: Algebra
samf-junior-2012-r2-06.body:
If the top-left number is $x$, the block is $x,\ x+1,\ x+7,\ x+8$ with sum $4x+16=312$, so $x=74$. (Indeed $74=7\cdot10+4$ is in column 4, so the block fits.)

**Answer: (D) 74**

samf-junior-2012-r2-07.title: Clear denominators
samf-junior-2012-r2-07.body:
The equations become $x-1=xy$ and $y+1=xy$. Both equal $xy$, so $x-1=y+1$, i.e. $x-y=2$.

**Answer: (A) 2**

samf-junior-2012-r2-08.title: Factors of a product of three primes
samf-junior-2012-r2-08.body:
$N=pqr$ with distinct primes. Its factors are $1,p,q,r,pq,pr,qr,pqr$, which is $2^3=8$ factors.

**Answer: (E) 8**

samf-junior-2012-r2-09.title: Find who is bigger than someone
samf-junior-2012-r2-09.body:
All numbers are positive, so we may divide inequalities by common factors: $bd<cd\Rightarrow b<c$; $bd<ab\Rightarrow d<a$; $cd<bc\Rightarrow d<b$; $ab<ae\Rightarrow b<e$. So $a>d$, $b>d$, $c>b$ and $e>b$: each of $a,b,c,e$ is larger than some other number, so none of them is the smallest. Hence $d$ is the smallest.

**Answer: (D) $d$**

samf-junior-2012-r2-10.title: Compare areas
samf-junior-2012-r2-10.body:
With radii $r,2r,3r$ the outer ring has area $\pi(3r)^2-\pi(2r)^2=5\pi r^2$ and the shaded centre has area $\pi r^2$. The likelihoods are in the ratio of the areas, $5:1$.

**Answer: (C) 5**

samf-junior-2012-r2-11.title: Name the groups
samf-junior-2012-r2-11.body:
Let $x$ be the number with chocolates only, so $2x$ have toffees only. Let $b$ be the number with both: $b$ is half of the class, so $b=x+2x=3x$. People with chocolates: $x+3x=4x$, of whom $3x$ also have toffees: the proportion is $\frac34$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac34$**

samf-junior-2012-r2-12.title: Speeds
samf-junior-2012-r2-12.body:
Take the distance as $20$ units: Olga's speed is $1$ unit/min and Dimitri's is $2$ units/min. Boris's speed is $\frac{1+2}{2}=1.5$ units/min, so he needs $\frac{20}{1.5}=\frac{40}3=13\frac13$ minutes.

**Answer: (B) $13\frac13$ min**

samf-junior-2012-r2-13.title: Count
samf-junior-2012-r2-13.body:
Alice turns over the $50$ even-numbered cards, leaving the $50$ odd-numbered cards face down. Brenda takes every third of these: the $3$rd, $6$th, $\dots$, $48$th of the $50$ remaining cards, i.e. $16$ cards. Face down: $50-16=34$.

**Answer: (D) 34**

samf-junior-2012-r2-14.title: Equations
samf-junior-2012-r2-14.body:
Let a bar cost $b$ and a packet of chips $c$. Then $2b+3c=19$ and $3c=2b+3$. Substituting: $4b+3=19$, so $b=4$ and $3c=11$. Jane pays $3b+3c=12+11=23$, i.e. R 23.00.

**Answer: (C) R 23.00**

samf-junior-2012-r2-14.title: Shortcut
samf-junior-2012-r2-14.body:
Jane buys one more chocolate bar than John. A bar costs $b$ where the $R19$ splits as chocolate $8$ and chips $11$ (the chips cost $3$ more than the chocolate, so chocolate $=\frac{19-3}{2}=8$). Two bars cost $8$, so one bar costs $4$ and Jane pays $19+4=23$.

**Answer: (C) R 23.00**

samf-junior-2012-r2-15.title: Compare lengths
samf-junior-2012-r2-15.body:
Let the circle have radius $r$. Peter travels $2\pi r$. The square is inscribed in the circle, so its diagonal is $2r$ and its side is $r\sqrt2$. Quentin covers $\frac{2\pi r}{r\sqrt2}=\pi\sqrt2\approx4.44$ sides. After $4$ sides he is back at $A$, and he has gone a further $0.44$ of a side along $AB$. So he is somewhere on $AB$.

**Answer: (B) somewhere on AB**

samf-junior-2012-r2-16.title: Triangular numbers
samf-junior-2012-r2-16.body:
The number $k$ occupies positions up to $1+2+\dots+k=\frac{k(k+1)}2$. For $k=12$ this is $78$ and for $k=13$ it is $91$. So terms $79$ to $91$ equal $13$, and the $81$st term is $13$.

**Answer: (C) 13**

samf-junior-2012-r2-17.title: Whole-number conditions
samf-junior-2012-r2-17.body:
Let there be $5x$ seniors and $3x$ juniors. Junior boys: $\frac35\cdot3x=\frac{9x}5$; senior boys: $\frac25\cdot5x=2x$. For the numbers of juniors in groups of $5$ to be whole numbers, $\frac{9x}{5}$ must be an integer, so $5\mid x$. The smallest is $x=5$: $25$ seniors and $15$ juniors, $40$ pupils (juniors: $9$ boys, $6$ girls; seniors: $10$ boys, $15$ girls).

**Answer: (A) 40**

samf-junior-2012-r2-18.title: Subtract a corner triangle
samf-junior-2012-r2-18.body:
Since $AC=\sqrt2$ and $AP=1$, $PC=\sqrt2-1$. The side $PQ$ is perpendicular to $AP$, so triangle $PCT$ (with $T$ on $CD$) has a right angle at $P$ and a $45^\circ$ angle at $C$: it is right isosceles with legs $PC=PT=\sqrt2-1$ and area $\frac12(\sqrt2-1)^2=\frac{3-2\sqrt2}{2}$. The shaded area is triangle $ACD$ minus triangle $PCT$: $\frac12-\frac{3-2\sqrt2}2=\sqrt2-1$.

**Answer: (C) $\sqrt2-1$**

samf-junior-2012-r2-18.title: Add triangles
samf-junior-2012-r2-18.body:
Triangle $APT$ has area $\frac12\cdot AP\cdot PT=\frac12(\sqrt2-1)$. By symmetry about $AC$ the shaded quadrilateral is made of $APT$ and its mirror image, so its area is $\sqrt2-1$.

**Answer: (C) $\sqrt2-1$**

samf-junior-2012-r2-19.title: Column analysis
samf-junior-2012-r2-19.body:
Let $X=100h+10t+u$, so $Y=100u+10t+h$ and $X+Y=101(h+u)+20t=1535$. Now $1535=101\cdot15+20$, so $20(t-1)$ must be a multiple of $101$, which for $0\le t\le9$ forces $t=1$. Then $h+u=15$ and the digit sum is $h+t+u=16$. (For example $X=619$, $Y=916$, $X+Y=1535$.)

**Answer: (E) 16**

samf-junior-2012-r2-20.title: Areas
samf-junior-2012-r2-20.body:
Each region has area $\frac13$. Triangle $ADQ$ is one of the regions, so $\frac12\cdot DQ\cdot1=\frac13$ and $DQ=\frac23$, $QC=\frac13$. By Pythagoras $AQ=\sqrt{1+\frac49}=\frac{\sqrt{13}}3$. The ratio is $AQ:QC=\frac{\sqrt{13}}3:\frac13=\sqrt{13}:1$.

**Answer: (B) $\sqrt{13}$**
